data.title: Crude oil price forecast as Brent hits $117 amid US-Iran war fears
data.description:
Crude oil prices continued their bull run, reaching its highest level since May as concerns about the escalation between the US and Iran grew. It jumped to $117, continuing a bull run that started in July when it bottomed at $70. This rally will likely continue rising in the coming weeks.

Brent and WTI jumps on rising US-Iran escalation fears

There are signs that the US, Iran, and Israel are planning a major escalation in the coming weeks. 

President Donald Trump has insisted that the US will not launch any attacks against Iran before the midterm election. 

Media reports suggest that the US and Israel are preparing a massive attack aimed at Iran’s civilian infrastructure. Trump and his officials believe that such a move will push Iran to capitulate and reach a deal. 

Israeli leaders have also planned to attack Iran’s oil infrastructure, a move meant to choke the country’s finances. A key target in these attacks will be Kharg Island, which handles more than 90% of Iran’s oil exports.

Iran, on the other hand, has warned that its response to any attacks will be more severe than before. It has warned that it will target energy infrastructure of its neighboring countries, including Bahrain, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates. 

Most analysts believe that the next phase of the war will be more destructive than previously. For one, Houthis, a less-equipped group than Iran has demonstrated its capability in choking Saudi Arabia’s oil facilities. 

Crude oil prices also continued rising as investors reacted to the ongoing Iranian attacks on ships crossing the Strait of Hormuz. The UKMTO issued a report of a ship that was attacked by an unknown projectile today, but open-source information is that more ships were attacked. 

Brent crude oil price technical analysis

Crude oil price chart | Source: TradingView

The daily chart shows that Brent has been in a strong rally in the past few months. This rally started after it bottomed at $70 in July. It has now crossed the important resistance level of $109.96, which coincided with the highest swing on September 11. Moving above that level was important as it invalidated the double-top pattern. 

Crude oil has remained above the ascending trendline that links the lowest swings since July. It also rose above the 50-day Exponential Moving Average (EMA), while top oscillators like the MACD and the Relative Strength Index (RSI) have continued rising. 

Therefore, the price will likely continue rising as bulls target the key resistance level of $120. It may even rally past that as the crisis in the Middle East escalates.

data.title: Rubrik stock hits a record high on AI demand, as a risky pattern slowly forms
data.description:
Rubrik’s stock extended its strong rally on October 23, reaching a record high as demand for cybersecurity solutions continues to grow amid the ongoing AI boom. Shares of RBRK jumped to $129.60, a 210% gain from their lowest point this year, lifting the company’s market capitalization to $26.9 billion. However, the stock appears to be forming a rising wedge pattern, which suggests it could pull back soon.

Rubrik stock jumps as demand for services rise

RBRK stock has been one of the best-performing stocks as the ongoing AI boom has led to a surge in demand for cybersecurity products. This demand has grown in the era of AI agents, which are expected to be the biggest threats in the world. 

The most recent results showed that its business continued to boom in the second quarter, with revenue rising by 38% to $427.3 million. Its subscription revenue rose by 37% to $407 million, a trend that the management expects will continue. 

Its customers paying at least $100,000 a year rose to 3,084, a 23% annual increase. Some of the biggest customers are companies like PepsiCo, Iron Mountain, and Adobe.

Analysts believe that the company has more room for growth. The average estimate among analysts is that its third-quarter revenue will be $430 million, up by 22% from a year earlier. Its guidance for the fourth quarter is expected to be $446 million, up by 18% from the same period last year.

Analysts are generally bullish on RBRK stock

Top analysts tracking Rubrik have a bullish outlook for the company. Dan Ives, who started Yorkville Ives, initiated the company with a target of $145, suggesting a 12% jump from the current level. 

Shrenik Kothari, a Baird analyst, boosted his rating to outperform, while Wedbush’s Steven Wahrhaftig has a target of $120.

The challenge, however, is that the stock has jumped above most of the analysts’ target. The average target among analysts is $115, suggesting a 12% drop from the current level. 

A major risk that Rubrik faces is its high valuation multiple. It has a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 240, much higher than the technology sector median of 21. Its forward EV-to-EBITDA stands at 227, also higher than the median of 13.

Rubrik stock technical analysis

RBRK stock chart | Source: TradingView

On the charts, we see that the RBRK stock has been in a strong upward trend in the past few months. It has jumped from a low of $41.73 in January to the current $130. The stock jumped above the key resistance level of $92.26, its highest point in December last year.

It has remained above the 50-day Exponential Moving Average (EMA), which has provided it with a strong dynamic support. The stock also remains above the Supertrend indicator. 

These technicals suggest that the stock has more upside to go. Such a move may push it to the resistance level of $150. The risk, however, is that the stock has formed a rising wedge pattern, which is made up of two ascending and converging trendlines. 

Rubrik’s MACD indicator has also formed a bearish crossover pattern. Therefore, there is a possibility that the stock will rise a bit, and then retreat as investors start booking profits.

data.title: Why Nvidia stock is in red today: growth case meets bearish warning
data.description:
Nvidia stock NVDA traded down 0.2% on Friday after falling 4.4% in the previous session, as investors weighed contrasting views on the chipmaker’s long-term prospects.

Seaport Research Partners reiterated a bearish rating, citing competitive pressures and financial commitments, while Laffer Tengler Investments CEO Nancy Tengler argued that Nvidia could still double in value over the next five to 10 years, even if earnings growth slows.

Jay Goldberg, an analyst at Seaport Research Partners, maintained a Sell rating and a $180 price target, below Nvidia’s Thursday closing price of $212.

He acknowledged that the company was positioned to deliver record sales in the near term but warned that challenges could become more significant over the following year.

Nvidia’s shares have climbed sharply in recent years, making it the world’s most valuable publicly traded company.

However, concerns about the sustainability of artificial intelligence spending have recently weighed on chipmakers and other AI-linked stocks.

Seaport flags competition and financial commitments

Goldberg identified four main risks to Nvidia’s outlook, including data centre construction constraints, financial commitments, circular financing and tensions involving smaller cloud infrastructure providers.

Although around 55 gigawatts of data centre capacity has been announced for the coming year, Goldberg said the industry may struggle to build more than 30 gigawatts because of shortages of electricians, gas turbines and utility connections.

He also warned that Nvidia’s commitments to securing its supply chain and supporting data centre construction total about $250 billion.

That figure excludes obligations connected to a funding initiative being developed with Wall Street, which Goldberg said could expand from $500 billion to $1 trillion.

Nvidia has the financial capacity to support these commitments, according to Goldberg, who expects operating cash flow to reach $200 billion this year.

However, he argued that such obligations could amplify the impact of a downturn.

Goldberg also raised concerns about Nvidia investing in and lending money to suppliers and customers.

He said credit guarantees and other financial support could effectively reduce customers’ costs, raising questions about underlying demand and competitive pressures.

Neocloud exposure creates strategic tension

Goldberg highlighted Nvidia’s relationship with neocloud providers such as CoreWeave and Nebius, which offer computing capacity as a service.

He argued that Nvidia benefits from having numerous smaller customers rather than relying on a few large cloud providers with greater bargaining power.

However, those smaller companies have taken on substantial debt amid uncertainty about the profitability of AI infrastructure.

“If the neoclouds fail to lift off, that doubles back on Nvidia with reduced sales and even more reduced margins,” Goldberg said.

He acknowledged that Nvidia could continue benefiting from strong demand in the near term, adding that the longer-term risks could take time to materialise.

Tengler sees room for further growth

Tengler offered a more optimistic view, arguing that Nvidia could double over five to 10 years even if earnings growth eventually slows to 20% or 30%.

She cited earnings growth of 96% and said she expected it to decelerate to 70% the following year before potentially settling at a slower pace.

These figures represent her outlook rather than company guidance.

Tengler compared Nvidia’s potential trajectory with Microsoft’s Azure cloud business, saying slower growth had not prevented the business from supporting the stock’s performance.

She also said Nvidia traded at a 13.5 earnings multiple when her firm added it to its value portfolio earlier in the summer.

That valuation reference was historical, not current.

data.title: Moderna leaked data was positive, what's hurting MRNA stock then?
data.description:
Moderna’s (MRNA) leaked cancer-vaccine trial results looked “promising” on the surface, yet the biotech stock came under intense pressure late on Thursday and was weak on Friday morning too, although the stock regained the losses and was trading higher later in the session.

In fact, MRNA slipped through its 20-day moving average (MA) this week, indicating bears have taken back control of the near-term.

Despite recent weakness, however, Moderna stock remains a blockbuster investment for 2026, currently trading at more than 6x its price at the start of this year.

Why Moderna stock keeps sliding?

The Phase 3 leaked trial data showed that “intismeran autogene” – Moderna’s personalized cancer vaccine – combined with Merck’s Keytruda reduced the risk of melanoma recurrence or death by 42% versus Keytruda alone.

It also lowered the risk of distant metastasis or death by 38%. Those are meaningful clinical gains, and the companies reported no new safety signals.

But the market had already rewarded the study’s success following August’s initial announcement.

The detailed findings therefore needed to improve expectations further.

Bloomberg reported that analysts questioned whether the melanoma results justified confidence in a much broader cancer franchise.

For MRNA shares, that distinction matters – demonstrating that one treatment works supports its development, while supporting a premium valuation requires a credible path to commercial revenue across a larger market.

Earlier trial created a difficult comparison

Another pressure point was the apparent gap with earlier research.

A smaller study showed a 49% reduction in recurrence or death and a 59% reduction in distant metastasis or death, compared with 42% and 38%, respectively, in the larger trial.

However, “different patient populations” and “follow-up periods” mean these are not really direct comparisons.

The latest findings also contain nuance that headline percentages miss.

The companies said the treatment groups performed similarly during the first six months; a prespecified analysis showed stronger benefits afterward. Overall survival data remain immature.

That makes sweeping conclusions premature. The study supports a reduction in recurrence, but it has not yet established an overall survival benefit.

Moderna investors assessing durability, treatment timing, and eventual adoption still have major questions to resolve as follow-up continues.

What’s the next test for MRNA shares?

Moderna’s next challenge is turning clinical progress into an economically attractive product.

The company is preparing to seek US approval and anticipates a potential launch in 2027.

Because the therapy is tailored to each patient’s tumor, investors will need to assess manufacturing capacity, delivery times, reimbursement, and the cost of supplying treatment.

Strong efficacy alone cannot establish the margins or sales volumes the business will ultimately generate.

Friday’s decline therefore raises a practical valuation question: how much future success does MRNA stock already assume at about 50x sales?

Regulatory progress, launch economics and evidence from additional cancer trials could help answer it.

Until then, a positive melanoma study can strengthen Moderna’s scientific credentials while still leaving shareholders vulnerable to falling expectations.

data.title: Oil crosses $116 as US reportedly prepares for prolonged Iran conflict
data.description:
Brent crude climbed above $116 a barrel on Friday, reaching its highest level since March, as investors assessed the prospect of a drawn-out confrontation between the United States and Iran alongside fresh threats to energy infrastructure across the Middle East.

The rally reflects growing concern that the conflict could continue disrupting oil supplies and shipping routes, adding to inflationary pressures worldwide.

The move came after US Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz told the Financial Times that Washington was prepared for a prolonged standoff with Tehran, potentially lasting another year if an agreement on Iran’s nuclear programme and the restoration of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remained out of reach.

US prepares for a prolonged confrontation with Iran

Waltz said the US could maintain its blockade of Iranian ports indefinitely while continuing to tighten economic pressure on Tehran.

The comments signal that Washington is preparing for the possibility that its objectives may not be achieved quickly, even as the administration hopes military pressure and sanctions will force Iran to make concessions.

Those objectives include addressing Iran’s highly enriched nuclear material and securing an agreement restricting domestic uranium enrichment.

President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have also renewed threats of a possible fresh offensive after the November 3 US midterm elections, according to the Financial Times.

The prospect of an extended conflict has kept traders focused on the risk that energy flows will remain vulnerable, particularly if military activity intensifies around major oil-producing areas and strategic shipping corridors.

Fresh attacks raise oil supply concerns

Brent crude rose as much as 2.8% to $116.32 a barrel on Friday while US West Texas Intermediate crude also advanced, trading above $101 a barrel.

The gains followed escalating clashes involving Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi movement and Saudi Arabia. Saudi Aramco ordered staff to evacuate its headquarters in Dhahran on Thursday as fighting intensified.

Separately, the United Arab Emirates reported an oil spill off its coast, adding to concerns about the safety of regional energy infrastructure and maritime traffic.

The developments have heightened concern about the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key shipping chokepoint at the entrance to the Red Sea.

Reuters also reported that a pipeline shutdown in Libya had reduced output from two oilfields, adding another potential source of supply tightness.

Prolonged disruption threatens to keep prices elevated

The oil rally has continued despite efforts to maintain and redirect energy shipments, with traders increasingly pricing in the possibility of further escalation rather than only current supply losses.

UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo told Reuters that volatile oil flows and elevated freight rates had left the market undersupplied, warning that renewed escalation could trigger further disruptions.

Brent was on track for a third consecutive weekly gain, while rising energy costs risk adding to inflation and complicating the outlook for central banks.

With no clear timeline for a resolution to the US-Iran confrontation, oil prices are likely to remain sensitive to developments around regional infrastructure, shipping lanes and the possibility of renewed military action.

data.title: Fed may hold in October, but analysts see a tougher call ahead
data.description:
The Federal Reserve is widely expected to leave interest rates unchanged next week, but the decision may offer little clarity on what comes next.

With inflation running above target, oil prices elevated and hiring showing signs of weakness, policymakers face competing reasons to tighten further or wait.

Futures-based estimates of CME FedWatch probabilities put the chance of a hold at 88%, against 12% for a quarter-point increase.

The Fed’s October 27-28 meeting follows its September rate increase, which came amid renewed inflation pressures.

A UBS note published October 19 also identified an unchanged October rate as its base case, followed by measured further tightening.

The firm said markets were pricing a more aggressive tightening path than it expected.

But the central question is not simply whether the Fed will hold next week.

Investors will be looking to Chair Kevin Warsh for clues about conditions that could prompt another increase in December, and whether the central bank is giving enough weight to employment risks.

Warsh’s communication strategy leaves markets guessing

Warsh has made clear that he does not intend to provide the kind of forward guidance used by previous Fed chairs.

Speaking in Bangkok on October 16, he said: “I don’t prejudge meetings. I don’t believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year.”

That approach is likely to make the statement, voting record, and press conference particularly important.

The October meeting will not include a new Summary of Economic Projections, which is published at selected meetings, leaving investors without an updated set of interest-rate projections.

Tracy Shuchart, Senior Economist at NinjaTrader, expects limited guidance from Warsh.

“He has been consistent since he took the chair that the Fed is out of the forward guidance business, he doesn’t prejudge meetings, and he still won’t submit a dot,” the economist told Invezz.

“Expect the same on the 28th. Anyone waiting for him to tee up December is going to be disappointed.”

Patrick Boyle, a visiting professor of finance and former hedge fund manager, said the wording of the statement could take on greater significance in the absence of forward guidance.

He suggested investors watch how the Fed characterizes the labour market.

A shift in its language from describing conditions as “solid” to saying they have “softened” could indicate that policymakers view the weak September employment report as more than temporary noise.

The voting record could also provide clues. Boyle noted that September’s decision was unanimous and said a dissent in either direction would offer insight into the committee’s debate over December.

JoAnne Bianco, Senior Investment Strategist at BondBloxx, similarly said markets should focus less on the immediate decision and more on whether the Fed leaves the door open to additional tightening.

“The more important question is whether Chair Kevin Warsh characterizes inflation as a temporary setback or evidence that policy needs to become more restrictive,” she told Invezz.

Oil prices raise questions about the source of inflation

The expected decision to hold rates comes against a difficult inflation backdrop.

US consumer prices rose 0.6% in September from a month earlier, lifting the annual headline inflation rate to 3.7% from 3.4%.

Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, rose 0.3% monthly and 2.6% annually, up from 2.4% in August.

Bureau of Labor Statistics data also showed that gasoline prices rose 9.1% in September.

Producer prices added to the concerns. The UBS note said September’s 1.3% monthly increase was the largest in four and a half years, exceeding the 0.5% consensus forecast.

Although energy accounted for much of the increase, UBS noted that prices rose across a broader range of goods and services.

Brent crude was trading near $113 a barrel on Friday, October 23, after a surge linked to renewed concerns about Middle East supply disruptions.

The challenge for the Fed is that higher interest rates cannot directly resolve a disruption to oil supplies.

Raising borrowing costs may instead weaken demand and economic activity, even as households and businesses face higher energy bills.

Shuchart said the Fed has repeatedly treated oil price shocks as transitory and indicated that monetary policy should look through them.

But she argued that September’s inflation report made that approach harder to sustain.

“The problem is the September CPI didn’t look transitory,” she said, pointing to the rise in core inflation and the possibility that energy costs were feeding into transportation services, airfares, freight and goods prices.

“The Fed is tightening into a supply shock with a hiring stall underneath it,” Shuchart said.

Rebecca Homkes, an Economist and Lecturer at London Business School, also highlighted the difficulty of using interest rates to address an energy shock.

“Interest rates are a crude tool for a complicated world, and an incredibly blunt one against the supply shocks driving price levels up,” she said.

But Homkes argued that the policy context makes it harder for the Fed to assume that an oil-related increase in prices will be temporary.

She referred to the Trump administration’s policy environment, saying that rather than simply looking through an energy shock, policymakers may have to anticipate further disruptions.

“With the Trump administration, it’s more ‘look for it:’ another shock will come soon,” Homkes told Invezz.

Robert R. Johnson, Professor of Finance, Heider College of Business, Creighton University, made a related but distinct argument.

He said that describing the inflation problem as an oil-driven shock assumes the pressure is transitory, while the war with Iran and the Trump administration’s tariff policy could continue contributing to higher prices.

Johnson told Invezz that both the tariff policy and the war were “unforced errors” by the administration, arguing that neither appeared close to resolution.

His comments challenge the idea that policymakers can treat the current inflation pressure as a single, temporary supply disruption.

In his view, the sources of price pressure extend beyond oil itself.

The implications for monetary policy remain uncertain. Homkes said higher rates can worsen a slowdown if supply shocks push firms to reduce hiring or investment.

At the same time, she said September’s inflation reading, economic growth and the latest personal consumption expenditures inflation data suggested that policy was not yet too restrictive.

A weak labour market complicates the case for further tightening

The inflation problem is only one side of the Fed’s dilemma.

The other is the labour market, where the latest report showed payroll growth falling short of expectations.

US employers added 29,000 jobs in September, compared with expectations of 90,000, while the unemployment rate stood at 4.2%.

Revisions to the July and August payroll figures reduced employment growth across those two months by a combined 60,000.

The BLS employment report showed that employment changed little across major industries.

Shuchart argued that the employment side is deteriorating faster than the inflation debate gives it credit for, pointing to weak payroll growth, downward revisions, an unemployment rate of 4.2% and negative real wages.

“That is not a labor market that absorbs a second hike quietly,” Shuchart told Invezz.

Bianco offered a more measured assessment. She said the labour market was cooling through reduced hiring rather than a meaningful increase in layoffs, describing the pattern as normalization rather than contraction.

“We do not think policymakers will place excessive weight on one weaker payroll report,” she said, adding that payroll data can be volatile from month to month.

Bianco said the Fed would likely need to see several consecutive months of weak payroll growth, a sustained increase in unemployment, slowing wage growth and broader weakness in hiring intentions before becoming more concerned.

That distinction matters for the December decision. A labour market that is gradually losing momentum may allow the Fed to wait for more evidence.

A sharper deterioration, however, could make another rate increase harder to justify even if inflation remains above target.

Johnson said the Fed’s dual mandate means policymakers must balance stable prices against full employment.

"The Fed has a dual mandate of stable prices and full employment, and it shifts its focus when one becomes more problematic than the other,” Johnson said.

He argued that inflation is currently the more pressing concern, while also noting that tighter monetary policy could weigh on hiring.

He added that the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown was shrinking the labour pool, offsetting some of the effects of weaker employment demand.

The competing assessments leave the Fed with little room for a simple response.

The latest inflation data support the case for tighter policy, while the employment report raises questions about how much additional pressure the economy can absorb.

December remains the central question

Markets continue to price in another rate increase by the end of the year, but the experts differ on how firmly that outcome should be expected.

Shuchart said the market has priced the December hike at close to 90%, but urged investors to “fade the certainty, not the direction.”

Her base case is a pause in October followed by another increase in December, although she cautioned that employment weakness could complicate that path.

Boyle also described a hawkish hold in October as his base case but said December remained genuinely open.

He said another increase would become more likely if core inflation continued to rise at a monthly pace of 0.3%, inflation expectations increased, and oil prices remained elevated.

A further weak payroll report, a rise in unemployment towards 4.4%-4.5%, or a resolution to the conflict that pulled oil prices back towards $80 a barrel would strengthen the case for a hold, he said.

Bianco said BondBloxx expects a December increase if inflation remains stubbornly above target, core inflation accelerates and the labour market remains firm.

Softer growth, moderating wage pressures or evidence that inflation expectations remain anchored would strengthen the case for no further move.

Homkes likewise said an additional increase should be expected if inflation stays hot, while emphasizing that the Fed must also consider whether policy is becoming too restrictive.

The data released between the October and December meetings will therefore be important.

Boyle identified the October and November employment reports and the October CPI release, scheduled for November 10, as key indicators.

The December meeting will also include an updated Summary of Economic Projections, giving markets a fresh view of policymakers’ rate expectations.

For now, the October hold is the clear market base case. What remains unresolved is whether Warsh will use the meeting to emphasize the need to contain persistent inflation or leave room to respond to a weakening labour market.

The post Fed may hold in October, but analysts see a tougher call ahead appeared first on Invezz

data.title: American Express beats earnings, cuts jobs - still fails to win over Wall Street
data.description:
American Express (AXP) posted a mixed Q3 and raised its annual profit guidance on Friday morning, but investors aren’t celebrating.

AXP shares came under pressure as the payments giant announced plans of eliminating about 5% of its global workforce.

The restructuring, intended partly to prepare the company for greater use of artificial intelligence, comes despite resilient spending among affluent customers.

For shareholders, the tension is clear: AMEX’s premium business keeps growing, but turning that growth into stronger profitability remains an expensive undertaking.

A key accounting distinction in AMEX’s Q3 earnings

American Express reported a 9% year-over-year increase in revenue to $20.06 billion on $4.68 per share of earnings.

Analysts had called for a lower $4.48 per share of earnings (EPS) but a higher $20.12 billion in revenue.

Investors should distinguish that performance from reported EPS of about $5.42 – which came in up 31% versus the third quarter of last year.

The adjusted figure removes the Global Business Travel Group stake-sale gain and associated restructuring charges, making it a more useful starting point for assessing continuing earnings power.

That said, the underlying demand picture remains rather encouraging. Card spending increased 8% to a whopping $454 billion, suggesting customers are still using their accounts actively.

Still, the revenue shortfall shows why healthy spending alone may struggle to lift AXP stock when expectations already assume considerable resilience.

AI-linked job cuts put premium-service model to test

American Express’ layoffs are part of an effort to simplify management, positioning the company for greater automation.

According to CFO Christophe Le Caillec, the goal includes becoming “leaner, more agile, and also to prepare for AI.” Amex recorded a $336 million restructuring charge in the quarter.

For investors, the potential benefit extends well beyond lower payroll costs – faster decisions and automated routine work could help the company expand without adding staff at the same pace.

But that opportunity carries an “execution risk.” Premium cardholders pay for dependable service, making customer experience a crucial constraint on cost cutting.

The investment case therefore depends on productivity improvements that preserve retention and service quality. A smaller workforce, by itself, does not establish that AI has delivered sustainable savings.

What’s the next catalyst for American Express?

AMEX now expects full-year adjusted EPS of at least $17.60 – and the financial services company remains on track for about 10% revenue growth.

Its credit metrics also offer reassurance: quarterly net write-off rate improved to 1.8% from 1.9% a year earlier.

However, lower credit-loss provisions partly reflected a reserve release, a benefit investors should avoid automatically projecting into future quarters.

That makes the next few quarters particularly revealing.

Investors should watch whether recurring earnings increasingly reflect business expansion and productivity, alongside continued discipline in lending.

Friday’s announcement offers a credible route to better profitability, but the valuation argument needs evidence that those benefits endure.

For prospective buyers, the most persuasive catalyst would be improving earnings quality while Amex protects the customer relationships that support its premium franchise.

data.title: JEPI yields 8%, SCHD yields 3%: which is the better dividend ETF?
data.description:
The JPMorgan Equity Premium Income ETF (JEPI) and the Schwab US Dividend Equity (SCHD) funds are popular among income-focused investors. JEPI has accumulated over $45 billion in assets, while SCHD has $116 billion in assets, making it the biggest dividend ETF in the world. So, which is a better fund to invest in?

SCHD ETF is firing on all cylinders on anti-AI demand

To a large extent, SCHD is not really a dividend ETF because of its low yield of about 3%. For example, the Vanguard Value ETF (VTV) yields 2% and is not considered a dividend fund. 

Even so, SCHD has become one of the best-performing funds in the world this year. It has had a total return of 32%, much higher than S&P 500’s 12%. 

The ETF has become popular among investors this year, drawing over $24 billion in inflows since January. Its popularity is mostly because it is made up of traditional companies that have little exposure to the AI industry. About 50% of its composition are companies in industries like healthcare, consumer staples, and energy. Technology companies make just a 14% of the fund. As a result, investors have rushed to its safety as fears of the AI bubble will burst escalate. 

Technicals suggest that the SCHD ETF has more upside to go. The daily chart shows that the fund bottomed at $32.37 on October 5 and then resumed the upward trend. It jumped to a record high of $35.35 on Thursday, moving briefly above the crucial resistance level of $35.30.

The risk, however, is that the fund has formed a double-top pattern whose neckline is at $32.37. This pattern often leads to a bearish reversal. However, there are signs that the ETF will continue rising, especially if it moves above the key resistance level of $35.50. A move above that level will point to more gains, potentially to $40.

SCHD ETF chart | Source: TradingView

JEPI has a higher dividend yield, but lags in performance

For many investors, JEPI seems like the better dividend ETF, thanks to its higher payout, which stands at about 8%. It also pays its dividends each month and has an exposure to the biggest companies in the United States, including popular names like Nvidia and Microsoft.

The fund uses the covered call strategy, where it invests in companies and then writes call options on the S&P 500 Index. It gets its dividends from the call premiums and the dividends paid by the companies. 

The challenge, however, is that, while the SCHD ETF has higher dividend yields, its total return is usually much lower than funds. Its total return this year is just 5.57% against the S&P 500’s return of 12.3%. In the last five years, JEPI has returned 41%, much lower than SCHD’s 62% and S&P 500’s 79%. 

Therefore, there is a likelihood that the SCHD ETF will continue doing better than JEPI in the foreseeable future. Indeed, history shows that covered call assets underperform their core assets. 

The post JEPI yields 8%, SCHD yields 3%: which is the better dividend ETF? appeared first on Invezz

data.title: Western Digital stock rises as strong earnings offset capex and supply concerns
data.description:
Western Digital WDC reported strong fiscal first-quarter results and issued an upbeat outlook as demand for hard disk drives (HDDs) continued to benefit from artificial intelligence infrastructure spending.

However, concerns about rising capital expenditure, potential increases in industry supply, and the sustainability of demand prompted mixed reactions from Wall Street analysts.

The company’s revenue rose 55% year over year to $4.38 billion, beating analyst expectations of $4.14 billion, while adjusted earnings per share reached $4.64, above consensus estimates.

Western Digital shares rose 1.06% on Friday.

The stock had more than doubled in value during the year through Thursday’s close, leaving investors to weigh the company’s strong operating performance against its valuation.

Analysts split over Western Digital’s valuation outlook

Morgan Stanley raised its price target on Western Digital to $668 from $643 and maintained an Overweight rating.

The firm described the results as a “strong, pricing-driven beat” and highlighted the company’s robust guidance for the December quarter.

However, Morgan Stanley also cautioned that “the market continues to be fickle".

UBS took a more cautious stance, lowering its price target to $435 from $470 while retaining a Neutral rating.

The firm acknowledged strong results and demand constrained by supply but warned that higher capital expenditure, accelerating industry supply and uncertainty about demand beyond the current cycle could put further pressure on the stock’s valuation.

Citi maintained its Buy rating, saying the results reinforced its positive outlook for the HDD storage cycle.

However, it lowered its price target because of a reduced valuation multiple for comparable companies.

Goldman Sachs also flagged valuation risks.

The firm said the shares could trade modestly lower despite strong results and guidance above consensus, citing elevated near-term capital expenditure and the possibility of competitors increasing capacity.

AI infrastructure supports demand and pricing

Western Digital’s results reflect continued demand for data storage linked to the expansion of AI infrastructure.

Chief Executive Irving Tan told analysts on Thursday that demand for the company’s HDDs remained strong and was increasingly coming from customers outside its traditional base, including neocloud providers and AI frontier labs.

The company’s blended average selling price per terabyte of storage increased 28% during the first quarter, indicating stronger pricing alongside higher revenue.

Tan said the company’s visibility into demand was extending further.

He added that Western Digital had visibility through 2030 or 2031 across its seven largest customers.

The outlook suggests that demand could remain supportive over the coming years, although analysts differ on how much of that potential is already reflected in the share price.

Strong second-quarter guidance and higher dividend

Western Digital expects fiscal second-quarter revenue of $5 billion to $5.2 billion, representing approximately 69% year-over-year growth at the midpoint.

It forecasts an adjusted gross margin of 60% to 61% and adjusted earnings per share of $5.60 to $6.

The company reported first-quarter profit of $1.78 billion, or $4.63 per share, compared with $1.15 billion, or $3.07 per share, a year earlier.

Western Digital also increased its quarterly dividend by 17% to 17.5 cents per share. The dividend is payable on December 17 to shareholders of record as of December 4.

The strong results and outlook underline the benefits of rising storage demand, but concerns over investment spending, competitive supply, and valuation continue to divide analysts.

data.title: Why is Bloom Energy stock falling on Friday despite Q3 earnings and revenue beat?
data.description:
Bloom Energy shares BE traded lower in trading on Friday despite the fuel-cell maker reporting third-quarter earnings and revenue well above Wall Street expectations, as investors weighed its aggressive spending on manufacturing expansion against concerns about cash flow.

The stock was down 9% during trading. Broader market weakness following a selloff in tech stocks on concerns that AI trade could be faltering likely also added to the pressure.

Bloom Energy reported earnings per share of 94 cents for the September quarter, up from 15 cents a year earlier and comfortably above the 69 cents expected by analysts polled by FactSet.

Revenue surged 138% to $1.24 billion, beating the consensus estimate of $1.07 billion.

The company also raised its full-year revenue guidance to between $4.4 billion and $4.6 billion, above the analyst consensus of $4.26 billion.

It maintained its adjusted gross margin outlook at 34%.

The revenue forecast has risen 41% since February, according to JPMorgan analysts, reflecting the pace of demand for the company's power-generation systems.

Record capital spending weighs on cash flow

Despite the strong results and upgraded outlook, Bloom Energy recorded its highest-ever capital expenditure in the quarter, contributing to negative net cash flow of approximately $180 million.

The company has been investing heavily to increase factory output and expand manufacturing capacity as it works through record backlogs.

Its spending is focused on solid-oxide fuel cell systems designed to supply electricity to large-scale artificial intelligence and hyperscale data centres, including Oracle's Project Jupiter.

The investment highlights the challenge facing Bloom Energy as it seeks to capitalise on demand for reliable on-site power while managing the costs of scaling production.

Its valuation also leaves limited room for disappointment, with the stock having gained more than 120% this year.

Investors are weighing the potential for continued rapid growth against the cash required to fund manufacturing expansion and customer deployments.

Analysts flag execution and valuation risks

BTIG lowered its price target on Bloom Energy to $250 from $295 while maintaining a Buy rating following the results.

This represents a 15% upside from Thursday's close.

The brokerage said near-term margin pressure could emerge as the company ramps up new production capacity and accommodates accelerated customer timelines.

While management sees a path to expanding manufacturing capacity to and beyond 5 gigawatts, the timing remains unclear.

BTIG said Bloom Energy remains positioned to deliver generation capacity, but the cost of adding manufacturing facilities is weighing on margins.

Oppenheimer maintained its Perform rating, citing concerns about cash flow as the company expands its customer asset base.

The firm highlighted a $430 million increase in Customer Assets and said investors may remain cautious until the cash conversion cycle for deployments becomes clearer.

However, Oppenheimer said it remained impressed by the scope and pace of growth, supported by the advantages of faster power availability, lower emissions and modularity.

AI power demand provides a longer-term opportunity

Bloom Energy has emerged as a beneficiary of the expansion of AI infrastructure.

Its solid-oxide fuel cells generate electricity through an electrochemical process rather than conventional combustion, attracting interest from cloud providers and data-centre operators facing rising power requirements.

The shares received additional attention after SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said on Wednesday that electricity generation and cooling infrastructure, rather than chip availability, were becoming the main constraints on expanding AI computing capacity.

"I think people are starting to realize the constraint on deployment of superintelligence is more in power and cooling and infrastructure than it is in chips," Musk said on the SpaceX earnings call.

Oppenheimer also highlighted Bloom Energy's potential in carbon capture, citing management's estimate of a $1 trillion total addressable market.

The brokerage said the concentrated carbon dioxide in the company's anode exhaust could help simplify capture systems and reduce costs, potentially allowing tax credits under Section 45Q to cover a substantial portion of expenses.

The opportunity could eventually provide additional revenue streams through server sales and other offerings.

For now, investors must balance that longer-term potential against the immediate costs of expansion and the company's ability to convert strong demand into sustainable cash flow.
